What did you do with it, and how did you evaluate whether it worked well for your use case?
detail: Drafted from your resume and used on the form: "At Arborphy AI, I worked with pretrained BioCLIP and DINOv3 representations for plant identification, treating them as foundation-model features rather than assuming they would transfer cleanly. I designed an EfficientNet–BioCLIP dual-encoder with bidirectional spatial cross-attention, auxiliary organ supervision, and BioCLIP-anchored gated residuals to test whether local visual features and BioCLIP semantics were complementary. I evaluated this with controlled fusion experiments: single encoders, concatenation, and uni- versus bidirectional attention; individual-disjoint, species-disjoint, multi-seed, and grouped held-out benchmarks; frozen linear probes; clustering; nearest-neighbor retrieval; and human review of hard cases. The main result was useful but humbling: fusion macro-F1 improved across iterations from 0.808 to 0.832, but under stricter evaluations I found no reliable species-recognition advantage over BioCLIP alone. That kind of evaluation discipline is what I would bring to Artera’s pathology foundation-model work.". To change it: jh answer answer:draft:e560fd89af "<your text>"

subject: Artera · Machine Learning Scientist, Computational Pathology: Describe a project where your model did not generalize as well as expected across datasets, sites, devices, populations, or other conditions. How did you investigate the problem, and what did you try to improve robustness?
detail: Drafted from your resume and used on the form: "In my current Arborphy AI work on plant identification, I expected an EfficientNet–BioCLIP fusion model to generalize better than BioCLIP alone, but grouped held-out and individual-disjoint evaluations showed no reliable species-recognition advantage. I treated that as a domain-shift question rather than just a tuning problem. I compared single encoders, concatenation, and uni- versus bidirectional cross-attention, then used frozen probes, clustering, nearest-neighbor retrieval, local PCA rotations, and centroid shrinkage to separate species signal from organ morphology and photographic-scale confounding. To improve robustness, I tried auxiliary organ supervision, BioCLIP-anchored gated residuals, individual- and species-disjoint benchmarks, and cross-model error review. That experience maps closely to Artera’s need for pathology models that hold up on messy real-world data.". To change it: jh answer answer:draft:7762bc1ea5 "<your text>"

subject: Artera · Machine Learning Scientist, Computational Pathology: Tell us about a machine-learning project where you had to understand or explain what the model was learning. What methods did you use, and what did you learn from them?
detail: Drafted from your resume and used on the form: "At Arborphy, I worked on a plant-identification model where the main question was not just whether fusion improved accuracy, but what each representation was actually encoding. I compared BioCLIP, DINOv3, and EfficientNet features using frozen linear probes, multi-seed clustering, nearest-neighbor retrieval, local PCA rotations, centroid shrinkage, and cross-model error review. I also ran controlled fusion experiments across single encoders, concatenation, and uni- versus bidirectional cross-attention, with individual-disjoint, multi-seed, and grouped held-out evaluation. The key lesson was that model behavior was partly semantic and partly geometric: DINOv3 carried strong organ-morphology signal, while BioCLIP remained the most reliable for species recognition, and added fusion did not produce a dependable species-recognition gain. That changed how I evaluated “better” architectures: interpretability and robust held-out behavior mattered more than architecture complexity.".
